title: Backtrackable Inprocessing
abstract: We introduce Backtrackable Inprocessing (BI), a framework that enables applying inprocessing under the current trail at any decision level, at any point during incremental SAT solving. Our approach lifts the long-standing restriction that inprocessing must be performed only at the global decision level, thereby substantially increasing its potential effectiveness. We focus on three highly efficient core techniques: subsumption, self-subsuming resolution, and Bounded Variable Elimination (BVE). We show how to ensure sound backtracking in the presence of inprocessing, and demonstrate that applying BI for incremental preprocessing after propagating assumptions yields significant performance improvements on Bounded Model Checking (BMC) benchmarks from the Hardware Model Checking Competition 2017. Implemented in the Island SAT solver (IntelSAT’s fork), BI enables solving ∼1.5× as many difficult bounds as the baseline global-level incremental preprocessor.

       Abstract
We introduce Backtrackable Inprocessing (BI), a framework that enables applying inprocessing
under the current trail at any decision level, at any point during incremental SAT solving. Our
approach lifts the long-standing restriction that inprocessing must be performed only at the global
decision level, thereby substantially increasing its potential effectiveness. We focus on three highly
efficient core techniques: subsumption, self-subsuming resolution, and Bounded Variable Elimination
(BVE). We show how to ensure sound backtracking in the presence of inprocessing, and demonstrate
that applying BI for incremental preprocessing after propagating assumptions yields significant
performance improvements on Bounded Model Checking (BMC) benchmarks from the Hardware
Model Checking Competition 2017. Implemented in the Island SAT solver (IntelSAT’s fork), BI
enables solving ∼1.5× as many difficult bounds as the baseline global-level incremental preprocessor.

 1      Introduction
Modern backtrack-search-based SAT solvers are widely used across numerous applications [5].
A SAT solver determines whether a Boolean formula in Conjunctive Normal Form (CNF)
is satisfiable. Since the introduction of MiniSat [9], incremental SAT solving has become
essential in many crucial domains [1, 2, 7]. In incremental solving, the user performs a
sequence of solver queries, each under a set of assumption literals (assumptions) [9, 15].
Clauses may be added before any query, and each query checks satisfiability of all clauses
provided so far under its specific assumptions. Implementations typically realize this by
assigning all assumptions as initial decisions (in order) and propagating after each assignment.
    Preprocessing [8] and, later, inprocessing [11] have long been known to significantly
accelerate SAT solving. Preprocessing simplifies the formula before search, while inprocessing
simplifies it regularly during search. One example of an inprocessing technique is subsumption:
if α and β are clauses with α ⊆ β, then α subsumes β and β can be removed. Initially
restricted to non-incremental solving, inprocessing was adapted for incremental use [16, 10]
and has been supported in the mainstream incremental SAT solver CaDiCaL [3] since [10].
    However, currently, inprocessing has a crucial limitation: it is applied only globally at
decision level 0. This restriction significantly limits the power of inprocessing. To illustrate
the limitation, consider the clauses α = a ∨ b ∨ c and β = d ∨ b ∨ c. At level 0, α does not
subsume β. But if we inprocess at level 1, after assigning a := 0, α does subsume β – until
the solver backtracks below level 1. Removing β at this point can be highly beneficial, as it
may trigger a chain of further simplifications. This motivates a natural question:

          Can inprocessing be invoked under the current trail at any decision level?

     No solver offers this capability, with correctness under backtracking the key challenge.

       1.1    Our Contribution: Backtrackable Inprocessing (BI)
       We introduce Backtrackable Inprocessing (BI), the first framework that enables inprocessing
       under the current trail at any level, at any point in the search. In this work, we focus on three
       core, extremely effective inprocessing techniques originally applied in the pioneering SatELite
       preprocessor [8]: subsumption, self-subsuming resolution (which we dub selfsumption), and
       Bounded Variable Elimination (BVE). BI fully supports incremental SAT solving.
           The key challenge is to ensure that the effects of inprocessing are tracked per decision
       level and can be soundly undone for any level we backtrack over, while remaining in effect at
       lower levels. We achieve this by generalizing how the solver classifies and manages clauses.
           SAT solvers classify clauses into two types: pervasive and temporary [18, 15]. The set
       (conjunction) of pervasive clauses is equivalent (or, in some solvers, equisatisfiable) to the set
       of input clauses, whereas temporaries are implied by the pervasives. Pervasive clauses must
       be preserved for correctness, while temporary clauses may be deleted at any time (at least
       at level 0) without affecting correctness and are therefore managed heuristically. Pervasive
       clauses begin as the input clauses but may change during solving; for example, if a temporary
       clause α subsumes a pervasive clause β, then β is removed and α becomes pervasive.
           We introduce additional clause types for BI, including:
           stashed at level i, which are deactivated until the solver backtracks below i, at which
           point they are restored;
           deputy at level i, which remain active and cannot be deleted until backtracking below i.

           As an example of how these clause types are created and managed, suppose α = a ∨ b ∨ c
       is temporary and β = d ∨ b ∨ c is pervasive under decisions e := 1 (level 1) and a := 0 (level 2).
       After detecting that α subsumes β as long as the solver does not backtrack below 2, we mark:

          β as a stashed-at-2 clause (deactivated),        α as a deputy-at-2 clause (active).

       When the solver backtracks below level 2, α will either be deleted or marked as temporary,
       and β will be restored as pervasive.
           In our framework, at all times, each deactivated stashed clause β has a deputy clause
       α that remains active and represents β (by implying it under the current trail) until either
       β is restored or another stashed clause γ that can represent β is restored. The correct
       management of stashed and deputy clauses is the core technical contribution of our work.
           To further clarify the role of deputy clauses, consider our example above but with α
       pervasive. Clause β would be handled as before (stashed-at-2 and reactivated as pervasive
       once the solver backtracks below level 2). The core difference is in the handling of α. In
       the original example, temporary α must be marked as a deputy to ensure correctness, by
       guaranteeing that α is not deleted and continues to represent β until β is restored. If α is
       pervasive, it simply remains so, since pervasive clauses are guaranteed not to be deleted.
           We implemented BI in the open-source Island SAT solver, a fork of IntelSAT [12]. While,
       in principle, BI supports any number of inprocessing steps at arbitrary levels, the empirical
       part of this work focuses on incremental preprocessing. We exploit the fact that BI can
       inprocess at the beginning of each incremental query after assumptions are set and propagated,
       rather than only at level 0 as in standard incremental inprocessing (e.g., in CaDiCaL [3, 10]).
       We implemented several BI-enabled incremental preprocessing strategies (Sect. 4.2.4).
           We focus on this setting because incremental preprocessing is the core performance-critical
       component in incremental SAT-based Bounded Model Checking (BMC). BMC plays a central
       role in hardware validation, where the goal is to verify the design for as many bounds as
       possible, and solving each new bound may mean the difference between discovering a crucial
A. Nadel                                                                                                    27:3


bug or missing it entirely. However, each unrolling to a new bound typically results in a
substantial increase in the complexity of the SAT instance, making progress toward higher
bounds increasingly difficult. Our experiments show that, on BMC benchmarks from the
Hardware Model Checking Competition 2017 [6], with a one-hour timeout per benchmark
and a bound threshold of 100, Island with standard global-level inprocessing solves 640
more bounds than vanilla Island without inprocessing, whereas BI enables solving 948 more
bounds, i.e., about 1.5× more of the difficult bounds unsolved without inprocessing.
   Below, Sect. 2–4 give preliminaries, introduce non-incremental subsumption-only BI, and
present full BI (proofs in the full version [14]); Sect. 5 and 6 report experiments and conclude.

 2      Preliminaries
We begin by recalling standard definitions from propositional logic.
▶ Definition 1 (Variables, literals, clauses, CNF). Let V be a countable set of Boolean variables.
A literal is either a variable x ∈ V or its negation ¬x. A clause is a finite set (disjunction)
of pairwise distinct literals. A CNF formula is a finite set (conjunction) of clauses.
     As is standard in the SAT literature, we represent the SAT solver’s search state by a trail.
▶ Definition 2 (Trail and decision levels). Let I be an input CNF formula. A trail is a finite
sequence of literals annotated with their decision level τ = ⟨ℓ1 @d1 , . . . , ℓk @dk ⟩, such that:
    all variables occurring in τ are pairwise distinct;
    the decision levels satisfy d1 ≤ · · · ≤ dk ;
    for each i with di > 0, we say that ℓi is a decision literal if there is no j < i with dj = di ;
    otherwise ℓi is an implied literal;
    writing Dec(τ ) and Impl(τ ) for the sets of decision and implied literals on τ , and for
    i ∈ {1, . . . , k}, Dec<i (τ ) := { ℓj ∈ Dec(τ ) | j < i }, we require that for every i with
    ℓi ∈ Impl(τ ), I ∧ Dec<i (τ ) |= ℓi .
                         V

In other words, in a valid trail every implied literal ℓi ∈ Impl(τ ) is implied by I together with
the decision literals appearing before ℓi .
    For the remainder of this paper, we fix the input CNF formula to be I and the trail to
be τ ; both are assumed to be given whenever referenced.
    As a direct special case of the trail definition at decision level 0, we get that all global
level-0 assignments are implied by the input formula; see Cor. 3.
▶ Corollary 3 (Global literals implied by I). Let τ = ⟨ℓ1 @d1 , . . . , ℓk @dk ⟩ be a trail. For every
i ∈ {1, . . . , k}, if di = 0, then I |= ℓi .
    A trail can be naturally interpreted as a partial assignment consisting of all its literals. For
the example trail τ = ⟨¬a@0, ¬b@1, ¬c@2, d@2⟩, we have τ |= (a∨b∨d) and τ ̸|= (a∨b∨¬d).
    We next extend our terminology to define satisfaction at a given decision level.
▶ Definition 4 (Restriction of a trail to level d). For a trail τ = ⟨ℓ1 @d1 , . . . , ℓk @dk ⟩ and
d ∈ N, define τ ≤d := ⟨ℓi @di | 1 ≤ i ≤ k, di ≤ d⟩, that is, the longest prefix of τ whose
decision levels are at most d.
▶ Definition 5 (Satisfaction at decision level d). Let φ be any Boolean formula and d ∈ N.
We say that φ is satisfied at level d if τ ≤d |= φ.
    We next introduce convenient notation for implication and equivalence evaluated at a
given decision level (relative to the fixed input formula I and trail τ ).

 3       Non-Incremental Backtrackable Inprocessing with Subsumption
This section introduces our framework for backtrackable inprocessing and its main algorithms
in the following simplified setting: non-incremental SAT solving with subsumption as the only
inprocessing technique. This restricted setting already captures the main ideas, terminology,
invariants, and algorithms. Section 4 then lifts these restrictions.
    We design our Backtrackable Inprocessing (BI) module to be integrated as a component
of a SAT solver with a clear API to the main search engine. The search engine interacts
with BI via the following two API functions:
 1. Inprocess: the main inprocessing function. It can be invoked after propagation has
    completed following either a decision or a conflict analysis, at an arbitrary decision level,
    and may be called any number of times during the SAT solver invocation.
 2. Backtrack: let m be the level at the end of the latest Inprocess or Backtrack invocation.
    Backtrack must be invoked once if the solver backtracks to any level below m.

       3.2    Invariants
       Fig. 1 summarizes the invariants jointly maintained by the main SAT search engine and our
       BI module. The BI module is explicitly designed to enforce these invariants, while they serve
       as requirements for the search engine. We will shortly argue that these requirements are
       natural for a standard SAT solver.

3.2.1     High-Level Invariants and Framework Correctness
Invs. 1 and 2 together guarantee the correctness of our framework: at any point during the
search, the active-non-temporary clauses N are logically equivalent to the original input
clauses I (up to level-0 simplifications implied by I). Strictly speaking, Inv. 2 ensures this
equivalence only until backtracking below level n, but maintaining this invariant during
backtracking is precisely the responsibility of our Backtrack procedure.

3.2.2     Low-Level Invariants
If Invs. 1 and 2 capture the high-level correctness of our framework, then Invs. 3 and 4
provide the corresponding low-level guarantees.
    Intuitively, Inv. 3 ensures that every stashed clause is represented until its restoration.
Unless it is trivially implied (trivial-representation), it is either represented by an active
deputy (deputy-representation) or by another stashed clause that will later be restored as such
a deputy (restored-representation). In the restored-representation case, at any concrete point
the stashed clause is still represented by an active deputy, but transitively: it is represented
via a chain of stashed clauses, the last of which is represented by an active deputy.
    Inv. 4 ensures that all clauses in the system are implied by the pervasive clauses.
    Lemma 13 shows that Invs. 3 and 4 imply Inv. 2 throughout the execution of our algorithm.
The proofs of this and all other lemmas appear in the full version [14].

▶ Lemma 13 (Correctness from representation and closure). Assume Invs. 3 and 4 hold. Then
Inv. 2 holds as well, i.e., N ↔n P .

3.2.3     Why the Search Engine Maintains All Invariants
We argue that a standard SAT search engine naturally maintains our invariants, both prior to
the first Inprocess call and between subsequent invocations of Inprocess and Backtrack.
Sect. 3.3 constructively shows that our BI module maintains them as well.
    We assume that the search engine itself does not apply inprocessing (which is instead
handled via interaction with our BI module), and that it performs only standard level-0
simplifications implied by the input clauses I, such as deleting globally satisfied clauses and
removing globally falsified literals. Throughout this section, all logical equivalences and
implications are understood modulo these level-0 simplifications, as justified by Cor. 3.
    Let us verify that our invariants (skipping Inv. 2 by Lemma 13) hold at the time of the
first Inprocess call by the search engine. Inv. 1 holds since, by construction, D0 comprises
the input clauses I up to the standard level-0 simplifications. Inv. 3 is vacuous, because
no stashed clauses exist before inprocessing. Inv. 4 holds since P comprises D0 , and A ∪ S
comprises D0 ∪ D∞ , where every temporary clause in D∞ is implied by D0 by construction.
    We now argue that the search engine maintains all invariants in each phase between
two BI invocations (Inprocess or Backtrack). Let n be the decision level of the latest BI
call. Crucially, during the phase, the level never drops below n, since Backtrack is invoked
whenever backtracking below n occurs. At the beginning of the phase, Invs. 1 and 2 imply
that I, P , and N are equivalent at level n, while D∞ is implied by these groups by Inv. 4.
The search engine operates only on the active clauses A = N ∪ D∞ , which, by construction,
remain equivalent to I at level 0 until the end of the phase. Hence Invariants 1 and 4 continue
to hold throughout the phase. As for Inv. 3, the stashed clause sets do not change, being
inactive, while deputy clauses may either remain unchanged or be simplified at level 0 (the
latter only if the solver allows level-0 simplifications at arbitrary levels). Such simplifications

       Our Inprocess algorithm is shown in Alg. 1. It operates in a loop. In each iteration, it
       selects a pair of distinct active clauses α ∈ Da and β ∈ Db with 0 ≤ a, b ≤ ∞ such that α
       subsumes β at some decision level, and this subsumption is minimal at level k. (If no such
       pair exists, the algorithm terminates.) The goal is either to delete β entirely whenever this
       is sound, or otherwise to stash β for as long as possible – that is, with the lowest possible
       restoration level – while ensuring that β remains represented until it is restored.
           Before presenting the algorithm in detail, we need a notion of rank; see Def. 14.

       ▶ Definition 14 (Rank of an active clause). The rank of an active clause γ ∈ Di is i.

          Promoting γ to a lower group (i.e., moving γ from Di to some Dj with j < i) does not

       all invariants in Fig. 1 hold. If we promote γ to some group Dj with j < i (by moving it),

           We now analyze one iteration of Inprocess by case-splitting on the relationship between
       β’s rank b and the minimal subsumption level k.

 4       Backtrackable Inprocessing
This section extends the subsumption-only non-incremental BI algorithm to support self-
sumption, BVE, and incremental SAT solving. With the theoretical foundations (clause
classification, invariants, correctness) already established in Sect. 3, we focus primarily on
the practical aspects of the algorithms.
    Our high-level inprocessing algorithm largely reuses incremental SatELite – the original
global level-0 non-incremental SatELite preprocessing algorithm [8], extended to global level-0
incremental preprocessing in our earlier work [16]. Sect. 4.1 reviews incremental SatELite
and related work, and Sect. 4.2 presents our complete BI algorithm.

        4.1     Incremental Preprocessing with SatELite and Related Work
        We start with standard definitions for resolution and selfsumption (self-subsuming resolution).

        ▶ Definition 20 (Resolution). Let α, β be clauses and x a variable. They are resolvable on x
        if x ∈ α and ¬x ∈ β. In this case the resolvent is α ⊗x β := (α \ {x}) ∪ (β \ {¬x}), and the
        resolution rule derives α ⊗x β from α and β.

        ▶ Definition 21 (Selfsumption, Strengthening). Let α, β be clauses resolvable on x. We say
        that α selfsumes β on x if α ⊗x β ⊆ β. Equivalently, writing α = C ∨ x and β = D ∨ ¬x,
        this holds iff C ⊆ D. In this case, β may be strengthened to D = α ⊗x β.

            For example, if α = (a∨x) and β = (a∨b∨¬x), then the resolvent on x is α ⊗x β = (a∨b),
        which is a subset of β. Hence α selfsumes β on x, and β can be strengthened to (a ∨ b).
            Finally, we use the term sumption to refer to subsumption and selfsumption together,
        and the verb to sume to indicate that a clause either subsumes or selfsumes another clause.
            Alg. 3 presents incremental preprocessing with SatELite [8, 16] in high-level, using the
        core data structures listed in Fig. 2.
            Consider the data structures in Fig. 2. The occurrence lists occ[ℓ] store all clauses
        containing literal ℓ. The clause heap H is a size-based heap used for efficient backward
        sumption to scan candidate clauses from smallest to largest to see whether they sume others.
        Finally, all eliminated variables are maintained in their elimination order in O (preserving
        this order is crucial for incrementality [16]), and for each eliminated variable v the original
        clauses are stored in F + (v) and F − (v).
            Alg. 3 is invoked at the beginning of every incremental SAT query. It first scans the clauses
        to initialize occ and H (line 1). Then, the loop in line 2 iterates over all eliminated variables
        in O. If new clauses containing a variable v have appeared since the previous invocation, the
        algorithm chooses to either reintroduce v by restoring F + (v) and F − (v) (optionally removing
        their resolvents) and removing v from O, or reeliminate v by adding the new clauses to F + (v)
        and F − (v) and creating new non-tautological resolvents, using the standard bounded-clause
        elimination heuristic to make this choice. Both reintroduction and reelimination may generate
        new clauses with eliminated variables, but, crucially for correctness, only with variables that
        will still be visited later in the current pass over O [16, 10]. The algorithm then enters the
        main preprocessing loop (line 5). It begins by applying backward sumption to a fixpoint
        (line 6). Next, every variable that occurs in clauses removed or updated during the latest
        sumption step is considered for elimination (line 7). A variable v is eliminated as long as
        doing so does not increase the clause count (line 8). Finally, elimination is applied only to
        pervasive clauses: temporary clauses are ignored, and, if elimination succeeds, any temporary
        clauses containing v are deleted.

        4.1.1     Other Related Work
        We reuse the high-level structure of incremental SatELite in our BI framework. Supporting
        gate extraction [8], as well as extending BI beyond sumption and variable elimination
        (in the spirit of [10], which achieves this for global level-0 inprocessing), is left for future
        work. We previously proposed incremental preprocessing after propagating assumptions
        in [17]. However, the present work is both significantly more general – our framework
        supports inprocessing at any decision level and at any point during solving, rather than
        only preprocessing at the beginning of each incremental query – and practically more
        useful, since [17] is closed-source (whereas our implementation is open-source) and relies on
        maintaining resolution proofs in memory, an infrastructure not supported by modern SAT
        solvers.

4.2      Incremental Backtrackable Inprocessing with Sumption and BVE

Throughout the rest of the paper, whenever we refer to level-0 notions (satisfaction, implic-
ation, equivalence, or subsumption with respect to τ ≤0 ), we call them global. In contrast,
notions at levels d > 0 (i.e., with respect to τ ≤d for some d > 0) are called conditional, since
they depend on the current trail.
    To integrate our subsumption-only BI framework from Section 3 into the SAT solver, it
is sufficient to:

1. Apply Inprocess (Alg. 1) for handling conditional subsumption directly as the imple-
   mentation of the sumption step in incremental SatELite (line 6 in Alg. 3), retaining the
   original processing order from smallest to largest clauses via the size-based heap, but
   ignoring conditionally falsified literals when computing clause sizes.

2. Stay synchronized with respect to backtracking: let m be the decision level at the end
   of the latest Inprocess or Backtrack (Alg. 2) invocation. Then Backtrack must be
   invoked whenever the solver backtracks below level m.


    Below, Sect. 4.2.1 defines conditional selfsumption and explains how to extend the above
BI integration in incremental SatELite to support it, while Sects. 4.2.2 and 4.2.3 show how to
handle conditionally satisfied clauses and BVE, respectively, within our framework. Finally,
Sect. 4.2.4 discusses the integration of incremental SAT solving (which comes for free in our
framework) and introduces several strategies for applying BI for incremental preprocessing.

4.2.3    Handling Bounded Variable Elimination (BVE)
We now turn to Bounded Variable Elimination (BVE). Unlike for sumption, there is no
“conditional” variable elimination, since the variable elimination algorithm itself does not
depend on the trail. However, the presence of conditionally satisfied clauses is promising for
bounded variable elimination efficiency-wise: skipping such clauses as described in Sect. 4.2.2
increases the chances of eliminating more variables while adhering to the clause-count bound.
For correctness, when those clauses are later restored, the relevant eliminated variables must
be reintroduced or reeliminated, but this is handled automatically as laid out below.
    Our BI integration preserves the standard BVE scheme of incremental SatELite, but, as
explained below, it introduces six easy-to-implement, BI-specific changes, mostly related to
assigning and managing ranks of original clauses and resolvents. Below, these changes are
numbered as (Ci) at the end of the sentences introducing them.
    In BI, new clauses containing eliminated variables may arise not only from the user (as in
standard incremental SAT), but also from restoring stashed clauses. Fortunately, incremental
SatELite (Alg. 3) already handles clauses with eliminated variables regardless of their origin.
We just need to ensure that the search algorithm invokes inprocessing whenever even one
clause with an eliminated variable is present in the solver, whether it is a user clause added
during a new incremental query or a restored stashed clause (C1).
    The remaining main question for handling BVE in BI is how to treat deputy clauses
during elimination and backtracking. Recall that a deputy of rank i (that is, a deputy in
Di ) is required only as long as the solver does not backtrack below i, at which point all
clauses in Di are deleted by Backtrack (Alg. 2). Therefore, conceptually, any resolvents
produced using such deputies become obsolete as soon as the solver backtracks below the
highest rank of their parents. To reflect this, we assign each resolvent the maximum rank of
its parent clauses as follows: when, while eliminating a variable v, we resolve α ∈ Di with
β ∈ Dj on v, producing the resolvent γ = α ⊗v β, we assign γ to Dk , where k := max(i, j)
(C2). Furthermore, we keep the original rank of every clause in F + (v) and F − (v) for any
eliminated variable v (C3). When the solver backtracks below level i, all clauses of rank i
are deleted from F + (v) and F − (v) for every eliminated variable v (C4). When a variable v
is reintroduced, the remaining clauses in F + (v) and F − (v) keep their rank when activated
(C5). Finally, as BI is designed to solve the problem under the trail, BVE attempts to
eliminate only unassigned variables, ignoring those already assigned on the trail (C6).
    Furthermore, following prior work on incremental inprocessing [16, 10], we restrict
elimination to variables occurring in newly added clauses; in BI, we further consider variables
appearing in clauses that contain literals assigned on the current trail, thereby avoiding
repeated elimination attempts for variables whose relevant context has not changed.

4.2.4    Incrementality and BI Strategies for Incremental Preprocessing
BI inherently accommodates clause additions and changing assumptions, so our framework
requires no modifications to support incremental SAT solving and can be applied as is.
   Although BI supports any number of inprocessing steps at arbitrary levels, we focus on
studying the effects of incremental preprocessing after the assumptions are propagated – a
minimal step that already distinguishes BI from standard global incremental inprocessing,
both in terms of algorithmic capabilities and in its empirical impact on Bounded Model
Checking (BMC). Below we present several strategies for incremental preprocessing.

             We call the first incremental preprocessing strategy enabled by BI the Assumption-Level
        (AL) strategy. It applies inprocessing immediately after propagating the assumptions for
        every incremental SAT query. As a baseline for comparison, we also implement a global-level
        BASE strategy that backtracks to 0 and preprocesses there with the assumptions frozen
        (i.e., not allowed to be eliminated) at the start of every incremental query (as in CaDiCaL [3]).
             Initial experiments on BMC instances showed that, although the BI-enabled AL is often
        more efficient, there are benchmarks where the standard global-level BASE wins. Further
        analysis revealed that the reason lies in how variables of literals implied by assumptions, and
        clauses that become conditionally satisfied under assumptions, are treated.
             AL ignores assigned variables and stashes conditionally satisfied clauses before inpro-
        cessing, which can be beneficial because less data is processed and BVE can eliminate more
        variables. However, there is a trade-off. First, eliminating variables that are about to be
        implied by assumptions can be helpful, and this is carried out by BASE but not AL. Second,
        AL misses selfsumptions by conditionally satisfied clauses that could remove falsified literals
        from other clauses, as illustrated below. Let α = (a ∨ b ∨ c) and β = (¬a ∨ b ∨ c) be clauses
        handled by AL under the trail τ = ⟨a@1⟩. Since α is stashed by BI as satisfied, AL misses
        the opportunity to strengthen β to (b ∨ c). While this does not affect reasoning under the
        current trail, any new temporary clauses that depend on β (including clauses selfsumed by
        β during inprocessing and learnt clauses during search) must carry ¬a, inflating the clause
        database and causing cache misses. In contrast, BASE would have strengthened β.
             Hence, we introduce a combined COMB strategy: immediately after a new SAT query,
        we first run inprocessing at level 0 (BASE) and then again after assigning and propagating
        assumptions (AL). This layered approach, despite its own overhead, can sometimes simplify
        the formula more effectively by first applying global and then conditional simplifications.
             Finally, we observed a clear pattern in when AL, BASE, and COMB work best. Let
        M be a measure of how intensively BI is used while AL is running. By default, we define
        M = number     of conditional selfsumptions

        Empirically, on instances with a small M , AL tends to be most effective (it is cheap while

                          6                       Conclusion
        We introduced Backtrackable Inprocessing (BI), a framework that allows inprocessing under
        the current trail at any level, at any point in the search, while preserving correctness under
        backtracking (focusing on subsumption, self-subsuming resolution, and BVE). We integrated
        BI into the Island solver and evaluated several strategies for incremental preprocessing on
        BMC benchmarks from HWMCC’17, obtained by unrolling each benchmark up to bound 100
        and using a one-hour timeout. Our best BI-enhanced strategy outperforms the baseline
        strategy, solving ∼1.5× more bounds among those unsolved without inprocessing.
            We have so far demonstrated BI’s benefit in incremental preprocessing; however, BI
        enables a much broader design space. Inprocessing can now be integrated into the search in
        many ways, paving the way for new strategies and significantly more efficient SAT solving,
        both non-incremental and incremental.
            Beyond SAT solving, BI is also promising for enabling inprocessing in state-of-the-art
        algorithms for model counting [19] and enumeration [20], which rely on systematic search
        without restarts and have therefore so far been unable to exploit inprocessing.
